items.passage: Meritocracy is an attractive idea. It promises that success will go to those who deserve it, to the talented and the hardworking, rather than to those born into privilege. The promise is so appealing that questioning it can feel like an attack on fairness itself. Yet the idea contains a quiet contradiction. Talent is not distributed by lottery alone; it is shaped by schooling, by health, by nutrition, by the books in a house and the networks around it. Effort, too, is easier when life is stable and harder when it is not. Two children of equal ability, born into different circumstances, will not have equal chances to show that ability, and the one who succeeds may sincerely believe the success was earned entirely by merit. The problem is not that talent and effort do not matter. They do, and a society that ignored them would be unjust in a different way. The problem is that meritocracy, by praising the winners, also blames the losers. If success is proof of merit, then failure must be proof of its absence, and the poor can be told that their poverty is their own fault. A fairer society would not abandon the idea of rewarding merit, but it would be honest about how much of success is luck, and it would refuse to use merit as a reason to abandon those who, through no fault of their own, started further back. The ladder may be real, but it is not the same length for everyone, and pretending otherwise makes the climb harder for those already at a disadvantage. Examinations are the clearest example, because they are designed to measure merit, yet they measure, in large part, the resources that went into preparation. A student who attends a good school, has a quiet room to study in, and can afford a tutor will perform better than a student of equal ability who lacks those things, and the examination will record the difference as a difference in merit. The system then rewards the first student with a place at a good university, which provides further resources, and the gap widens. None of this means examinations should be abolished, but it means their results should be read with humility, as a measure of performance under unequal conditions, not as a verdict on a person's worth, and a society that forgets that distinction will mistake privilege for talent.

items.passage: Language is often treated as a neutral tool, a way of describing a world that exists independently of words. Yet the words we choose decide what can be said, and therefore what can be thought. To call a tax cut relief is to imply that tax is an affliction, and that cutting it is a cure. To call civilian deaths collateral damage is to make them sound like an unavoidable side effect, rather than a moral catastrophe. To call a firing a downsizing is to hide the human cost behind a technical term. None of this is accidental. Those who control the terms of a debate often control its outcome, because the terms decide which questions are legitimate and which are ruled out before they are asked. Power, in this account, is not only exercised through laws and armies. It is exercised through vocabulary, through the slow work of making some descriptions seem natural and others seem extreme. The remedy is not to find a perfectly neutral language, since no such language exists, but to notice the work that words are doing. When a phrase feels inevitable, ask who benefits from its inevitability. When a euphemism smooths over a harm, ask what the plain description would sound like. Language will always shape thought, but thought can also, with effort, reshape language, and that effort is one of the few defences a society has against being governed by words it did not choose. News headlines show the same mechanism at work every day, because a headline must compress a complex event into a few words, and the words chosen decide how the event is understood. A protest can be described as a riot or as a demonstration, a tax as a burden or as a contribution, a migrant as a stranger or as a neighbour, and each choice frames the story before the reader has read a single sentence. Readers who are aware of this can seek out other framings, compare them, and form a judgement that is their own. Readers who are not aware may believe they are forming an opinion, when in fact they are repeating the framing they were given, and that is why media literacy, the ability to notice the work words are doing, is now as important as the ability to read them.

Every headline that uses a metaphor is deliberately lying to its readers.
To call a tax cut relief is to imply that tax is an affliction, and to call civilian deaths collateral damage is to make them sound like an unavoidable side effect.

Language shapes thought by deciding what can be said and thought, so power is exercised through vocabulary, and the defence is to notice the work words do, ask who benefits, and ask what the plain description would sound like.
items.explanation: The correct option joins both limbs of the argument. The two half-right options each capture only one limb and drop the other, the overclaim goes beyond what the author argues, and the single-claim option restates one supporting point rather than the argument as a whole.

items.passage: Climate change is often discussed as a technical problem, a matter of parts per million and degrees of warming. Yet its deepest questions are moral. Those who have emitted least, farmers in low lying deltas, herders in drying grasslands, islanders whose homes may disappear, are often those who will suffer most. Those who have emitted most, wealthy societies with air conditioning, insurance and the means to move, are often best protected from the consequences of their own emissions. This asymmetry is what makes climate policy so difficult. It is not only a question of how much to cut, but of who should cut, who should pay, and who should decide. A policy that asks the poorest to bear the cost of a crisis they did not cause is not merely inefficient; it is unjust. A policy that asks the richest to pay for the damage they caused is not merely fair; it is also the only kind that the poorest will accept as legitimate. The difficulty is that the rich, who must pay, are also those with the most power to resist paying, while the poor, who must be protected, have the least power to demand protection. Justice, in this context, is not an extra demand added to climate policy. It is the condition without which climate policy cannot work, because a policy perceived as unjust will be resisted, evaded and ultimately abandoned, while a policy perceived as fair has a chance of being sustained across the decades that climate action requires. Adaptation funding raises the same question in practical form, because the money for sea walls, for drought resistant crops and for relocating villages must come from somewhere, and the countries that need it most are often those least able to pay for it. A fund that is financed by voluntary contributions from wealthy countries may be generous in good years and empty in bad ones, while a fund financed by a levy on emissions would be more stable, but harder to agree. The choice between those designs is not technical but moral, because it decides who bears the cost of a crisis, and whether the burden falls on those who caused it or on those who suffer from it. A climate policy that ignores that choice may succeed on paper, by cutting emissions, while failing in practice, by losing the consent of those it was meant to protect.
items.question: Which of the following best captures the author's central argument?
options: Climate change is only a technical problem, so the distribution of its costs does not affect whether policy succeeds.
The poorest should bear the cost of the crisis, because they are the ones who will suffer most from it.
No climate policy has ever been resisted by anyone for reasons of fairness.

Climate change is a moral problem of asymmetry, because those who emitted least suffer most and those who emitted most can resist paying, so justice is the condition of workable policy rather than an extra demand added to it.
Those who have emitted least are often those who will suffer most from climate change, while those who have emitted most are often best protected from the consequences.
items.explanation: The correct option joins both limbs of the argument. The two half-right options each capture only one limb and drop the other, the overclaim goes beyond what the author argues, and the single-claim option restates one supporting point rather than the argument as a whole.

items.question: Which of the following pairs of claims is supported by the passage?

(i) The richest emit least and suffer most. (ii) Adaptation funding should come only from voluntary contributions.
(i) Climate policy is only a technical problem of parts per million. (ii) The rich have the least power to resist paying.
(i) A voluntary fund is more stable than a levy fund. (ii) Justice is the condition without which climate policy cannot work.
items.explanation: The passage says a policy that asks the richest to pay is the only kind the poorest will accept as legitimate, which supports claim (i) of option B, and it says a policy perceived as unjust will be resisted, evaded and ultimately abandoned, which supports claim (ii). Option A pairs a true first claim with a second claim the passage explicitly denies, since justice is not an extra demand. Option C reverses the facts on both halves. Option D contradicts the passage on both halves. Option E pairs a reversed first claim with a true second claim, so the pair as a whole is not supported.

items.question: Which of the following conclusions would the author most likely endorse?
options: No climate policy has ever been resisted by anyone for reasons of fairness.
Wealthy societies will always pay willingly for climate damage, so no enforcement is ever needed.

Adaptation funding must be judged by who bears the cost, and a levy on emissions is more stable than voluntary contributions, because the design decides whether the burden falls on those who caused the crisis or on those who suffer from it.
Climate change is only a technical problem, so the distribution of its costs does not affect whether policy succeeds.
Justice is the only thing that matters in climate policy, and any policy that cuts emissions without addressing justice is worthless.
items.explanation: Only the third option is fully supported by the passage. The passage says a fund financed by a levy on emissions would be more stable than one financed by voluntary contributions, and that the choice of design decides who bears the cost of the crisis and whether the burden falls on those who caused it or on those who suffer from it. The rewritten fifth option overclaims: the passage treats justice as a condition for policy to work and allows that a policy may succeed on paper by cutting emissions while failing in practice, which is not the same as saying justice is the only thing that matters or that such a policy is worthless. The first option is an absolute claim the passage never makes, the second contradicts the passage's point that the rich have the most power to resist paying, and the fourth contradicts the passage's central claim that climate change is a moral problem and not only a technical one.

items.passage: Surveillance is often defended on the grounds that it catches criminals, and that the innocent have nothing to hide. That defence misses the deeper effect of being watched. A person who knows she may be watched behaves differently from a person who knows she is alone, even when she has done nothing wrong. She chooses her words more carefully, avoids unpopular opinions, and thinks twice before reading something unusual. The watcher need not punish anyone for this effect to occur; the possibility of being watched is enough. Over time, the effect becomes internal. People stop needing an external watcher, because they have internalised one, censoring themselves before any authority intervenes. A society in which everyone behaves as if watched is not necessarily a safer society. It may be a quieter one, but quiet is not the same as safety, and a society that has lost the habit of dissent, of experiment, of saying the unpopular thing, has lost something that safety alone cannot replace. Privacy, in this account, is not a luxury for those with secrets to hide. It is the condition that allows people to think, to doubt and to dissent without fear, and without it, freedom becomes a performance, something people do when they believe they are being observed, rather than something they possess when they are alone. Workplace monitoring extends the same logic into offices and factories, where keystrokes, locations and even eye movements can be tracked in the name of productivity. An employee who knows she is monitored may work faster, but she may also avoid taking risks, avoid asking questions, and avoid the informal conversations in which new ideas are born. The organisation gains a measure of activity and loses a measure of creativity, and it may not notice the loss, because creativity is harder to count than keystrokes. A wiser employer would monitor outcomes rather than movements, trusting employees to find their own way to a result, and would accept that some unmonitored time is not wasted time but the space in which thinking happens, and in which a worker can be alone with a problem long enough to solve it.

items.passage: In an age of perfect reproduction, the question of authenticity has become urgent. A photograph can be copied a million times without loss, a painting can be reproduced so accurately that experts struggle to tell the copy from the original, and a piece of music can be heard in exactly the same form by listeners on opposite sides of the world. Why, then, does the original still matter? Part of the answer is history. The original was present at a moment that cannot be repeated; it bears the marks of the hand that made it, the accidents of its creation, the repairs of centuries. A copy, however perfect, has a different history, and that history matters to how we value it. Another part is scarcity. An original is one of a kind, while a copy can be multiplied without limit, and scarcity, for better or worse, shapes desire. But the deepest part is human. We value the original because it is a trace of another person, a proof that someone was there, that a hand moved in a particular way at a particular time. A copy can show us what the original looks like, but it cannot show us that it was made. Authenticity, in this account, is not a property of the image alone. It is a property of the relationship between the object, its maker and its history, and that relationship cannot be reproduced, however perfect the copy. Digital art raises the question in a new form, because a digital image can be copied perfectly and distributed instantly, yet artists now sell certificates of authenticity that claim a particular copy is the original. The certificate does not change the image, which remains identical to every other copy, but it changes the relationship between the owner, the artist and the work, creating scarcity where none existed before. Some see this as a clever solution to an old problem, a way for digital artists to earn a living. Others see it as a sign that authenticity has become a fiction, a story told about an object rather than a property of it. Either way, the debate shows that authenticity was never only about the object itself, but about the human relationships that surround it, and those relationships can be created, bought and sold, even when the image cannot be distinguished from its copies.

The original was present at a moment that cannot be repeated, bears the marks of the hand that made it, and has a history that a copy, however perfect, does not share.

items.passage: Her hands remembered what her mind had forgotten, / the pattern of the border, the twist of the thread, / the way the shuttle moved when the light was low, / and the cloth grew, row by row, in the quiet room. // She did not count the threads, or name the colours, / and the shuttle flew like a bird that knows its way, / returning always to the hand that had thrown it. // The cloth she wove was not for sale, or for show, / it was for the daughter who had gone away, / for the winter that would come, for the hands / that would one day hold it and remember her. // When she died, the cloth remained, / folded, in a drawer, smelling of woodsmoke, / and her daughter, holding it, understood at last / that some things are not taught, but woven, / in the hands, in the quiet, in the work itself.
items.question: Which of the following correctly pairs a reading of the image of the shuttle flying like a bird that knows its way, returning always to the hand that threw it with the later line that confirms it?
options: The weaver owned a pet bird that lived in the weaving room; "the shuttle flew like a bird that knows its way"
The weaver threw the shuttle carelessly and it often got lost; "returning always to the hand that had thrown it"
Skill lives in the hands as a learned rhythm that needs no counting or naming, returning surely because it was practised into the body; "the cloth she wove was not for sale, or for show"
The cloth is only a household object with no meaning beyond its use; "that some things are not taught, but woven, in the hands, in the quiet, in the work itself"

Skill lives in the hands as a learned rhythm that needs no counting or naming, returning surely because it was practised into the body; "that some things are not taught, but woven, in the hands, in the quiet, in the work itself"
items.explanation: The shuttle's sure return is embodied skill, not luck; and the cloth kept for the absent daughter is how the mother remains present. The confirming line is the one that says some things are not taught but woven, in the hands, in the quiet, in the work itself, which is exactly the reading of the shuttle. The line about the cloth not being for sale concerns the cloth's purpose, not the shuttle's rhythm, so it does not confirm the skill reading, and the line about returning always contradicts carelessness.

items.question: Which reading captures both the shuttle's flight and the cloth that is not for sale?
options: The weaver was poor and could not afford to sell her cloth in a market
Skill lives in the hands as a practised rhythm, but the cloth is only a household object with no meaning beyond its use
The cloth carries the maker to the daughter, but the shuttle's flight shows the weaver worked carelessly and without skill
Some things are not taught but woven, in the hands, in the quiet, in the work itself, so that the cloth carries the maker to the daughter after her death
The daughter went away because she disliked the cloth her mother wove
items.explanation: The poem joins two images. The shuttle flies like a bird that knows its way, returning always to the hand that threw it, which says skill lives in the hands as a learned rhythm that needs no counting or naming. The cloth is not for sale or for show but for the daughter who has gone away, which says the work carries the maker to the daughter after her death. Only the fourth option holds both images together. The second keeps the shuttle but empties the cloth of meaning, the third keeps the cloth but misreads the shuttle as carelessness, and the first and fifth invent motives the poem never gives.

items.question: A school finds that students who attend extra tuition score higher in final exams than those who do not. The headteacher concludes that extra tuition raises scores. Which of the following, if true, most weakens the conclusion?
options: Most students say they enjoy extra tuition, and attendance at the sessions is high
A few students who attend tuition still score poorly, while some who never attend score very well
The students who attend extra tuition are those whose parents can afford it and who already score higher, because they also have quiet study rooms and private tutors at home
Extra tuition costs less than repeating a year of school
Scores also rose in a year when the exam was made easier for everyone
items.explanation: If tuition takers are already advantaged and higher scoring, the association reflects who takes tuition rather than what tuition does. Enjoyment, a few exceptions and cost do not test the causal claim.

items.question: A restaurant introduces a new menu and finds that customer satisfaction rises by 15 percent in two months. The owner concludes the new menu caused the rise. Which of the following, if true, most weakens the conclusion?
options: Some customers praised the new dishes, while a few said they preferred the old menu
In the same two months the restaurant replaced its slowest, rudest waiter, whose behaviour had been the main source of complaints, so satisfaction would have risen under any menu
Satisfaction also rose at a second branch that kept the old menu, but that branch also replaced its rudest waiter in the same month
The new menu cost little to design and used cheaper ingredients
A rival restaurant that changed its menu saw satisfaction fall after a price rise
items.explanation: Replacing the waiter who caused most complaints is an alternative cause that fully accounts for the rise. The second branch also replaced its waiter, so its rise is consistent with that explanation rather than a second weaken.

items.question: A study finds that people who read for pleasure every day have larger vocabularies than people who never read. The readers also tend to have more years of schooling and jobs that involve writing. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: Reading for pleasure may or may not enlarge vocabulary, because readers differ from non-readers in schooling and in the demands of their jobs
Reading for pleasure definitely enlarges vocabulary, because readers have larger vocabularies
Reading for pleasure has no effect on vocabulary, because schooling fully explains the difference
People who never read cannot have a large vocabulary under any circumstances
Schooling has no effect on vocabulary, so reading must be the cause
items.explanation: Schooling and job demands are confounders that could explain the vocabulary difference. The study cannot isolate reading's effect, so neither a definite causal claim nor a definite no-effect claim follows.

items.question: Choose the sentence in which BOTH words in capitals are used correctly.
options: The critic called the first play DERIVATIVE, because it was the first of its kind and invented a whole new form, and the second play ORIGINAL, because every scene copied a famous earlier play.

The critic called the first play DERIVATIVE, because every scene copied a famous earlier play without adding anything new, and the second play ORIGINAL, because every scene copied a famous earlier play.
The critic called the first play DERIVATIVE, because it was the first of its kind and invented a whole new form, and the second play ORIGINAL, because no earlier play had done anything like it.
Her DERIVATIVE cooking used only ingredients she had grown herself, and her ORIGINAL recipe was copied word for word from a book.

The critic called the first play DERIVATIVE, because every scene copied a famous earlier play without adding anything new, and the second play ORIGINAL, because no earlier play had done anything like it.
items.explanation: DERIVATIVE means copied and unoriginal, and ORIGINAL means new and inventive. Only the last option uses both correctly: copying every scene without adding anything new is derivative, and doing what no earlier play had done is original. The first option misuses both, the second misuses ORIGINAL, the third misuses DERIVATIVE, and the fourth misuses both, since home-grown ingredients do not make cooking derivative and a copied recipe is not original.

items.question: Consider the following six sentences. (1) The number of applicants have doubled since last year. (2) Neither the players nor the captain was blamed for the defeat. (3) The jury were unanimous in its verdict. (4) Each of the houses in the street has a small garden. (5) A number of questions remains unanswered. (6) The staff is unhappy with the new working hours. Which of the following combinations consists entirely of correct sentences?
options: Sentences 1, 2 and 4
Sentences 1, 2 and 6
Sentences 1, 4 and 6
Sentences 2, 4 and 6
Sentences 1, 3 and 5
items.explanation: Sentences 2, 4 and 6 are correct: neither-nor with a singular nearer subject takes a singular verb, each of takes a singular verb, and staff as a single body takes a singular verb. Sentence 1 needs has, sentence 3 needs was, and sentence 5 needs remain.

items.question: Rearrange the following sentences to form a coherent paragraph. (A) The bank's new app was downloaded a million times in its first month. (B) That figure impressed the board, which had expected half as many downloads. (C) It did not impress the customers, most of whom deleted the app within a week. (D) They did so because the app crashed whenever they tried to transfer money, the one task most of them needed. (E) The lesson the bank learned, at considerable cost, is that downloads measure curiosity, not satisfaction. Which of the following is the correct order?
options: C-A-B-D-E
D-B-C-A-E
A-B-C-D-E
A-B-E-C-D
E-A-B-C-D
items.explanation: A gives the downloads, B gives the board's reaction, C contrasts it with the customers' reaction, D explains why they deleted it, and E draws the lesson. D's they did so needs C's deletion before it, and E's lesson needs the whole contrast.

items.question: Rearrange the following sentences to form a coherent paragraph. (A) The river that runs through the town has been measured every day for ninety years. (B) Those measurements show a slow, steady fall in the water level, of about a centimetre a year. (C) That fall, small in any single year, amounts over ninety years to almost a metre of lost water. (D) The town has noticed the loss only recently, when wells that had never run dry began to fail. (E) Slow change, in other words, is easy to ignore until the day it can no longer be ignored. Which of the following is the correct order?
options: C-A-B-D-E
A-B-C-D-E
D-B-C-A-E
A-B-E-C-D
E-A-B-C-D
items.explanation: A introduces the measurements, B states what they show, C's that fall needs B before it, D gives the town's late noticing, and E generalises. C before B would leave that fall without an antecedent.

items.question: The inspectors' report was ______ in its praise of the school's pastoral care, which parents described as exceptional; ______ in its judgement of the teaching of mathematics, where results had fallen for three years; and ______ in its overall grade, commending the school in one breath and placing it under review in the next.
options: fulsome; damning; equivocal
fulsome; approving; equivocal
muted; damning; equivocal
fulsome; damning; glowing
muted; approving; glowing
items.explanation: The three blanks interact, and the third can only be fixed from the first two together. Praise of care described as exceptional is fulsome, not muted, and results that had fallen for three years make the judgement of mathematics damning, not approving. An overall grade that commends the school and places it under review at the same time is equivocal, not glowing. The sentence gives no explicit contrast word, so the equivocal grade has to be inferred from the praise and the criticism. Each distractor fails exactly one blank, except the last, which fails all three.

items.question: The cartoon shows a judge weighing two objects on a pair of scales: on one side a feather labelled Mercy, on the other a stone labelled Justice. The scales are perfectly balanced, but the judge looks worried. Which of the following best captures the meaning of the cartoon?
options: A feather is lighter than a stone, so the cartoon shows the scales are broken
Judges should always choose mercy, because justice is too heavy to carry
The cartoon proves that justice and mercy can never be balanced at all
The judge is worried because the scales are too old and need replacing
Justice and mercy must be held in balance, and the judge's worry shows that balancing them is a difficult judgement rather than a mechanical weighing
items.explanation: The scales balance, yet the judge worries, because the balance is a judgement to be made, not a mechanical result. The cartoon is about the difficulty of holding justice and mercy together, not about the physical weights.

If the largest customer has already secured supply elsewhere, the firm can allocate scarce chips to smaller customers without losing its biggest account, which supports a fair allocation. A rival raising prices is a separate market fact. The chip maker offering a priority fee is a temptation, not a reason to favour one customer. The contract requiring equal treatment supports fairness but is a rule, not the commercial reason. A new chip design arriving later does not solve this quarter's shortage.
options: A rival firm has raised its prices because of the same shortage
The chip maker has offered a priority supply fee for faster delivery
The supply contract requires equal treatment of all customers
The largest customer has already secured an alternative supply for this quarter and will not be affected by a delay
A new chip design that uses fewer chips will be ready next year
items.passage: A maker of smart home devices needs a specialised chip that is now in short supply worldwide after a factory fire in another country. The firm has enough chips for only 40 percent of its planned production this quarter, and it must decide how to allocate them. Its largest customer, a retail chain, has ordered 50 percent of the planned output and is threatening to cancel all future orders if the firm does not meet the order in full. Three smaller customers, who together ordered 30 percent, have been loyal for years but have no alternative supplier. The remaining 20 percent is for the firm's own online store, which earns the highest margin per unit. The sales head wants to give all available chips to the largest customer to protect the relationship, arguing that losing the chain would cost the firm half its revenue. The operations head argues for a fair allocation across all customers, warning that abandoning loyal smaller customers will destroy trust and that the chain will return once supply recovers. The finance head notes that the online store earns the highest margin, so allocating chips there would protect profit. The chief executive must decide this week, because the chip shipment arrives on Monday and production planning cannot wait. The firm's 200 dealers have paid for showroom branding and have promised customers delivery dates that depend on the chip shipment arriving on Monday. The chip maker has said the next shipment will arrive in six weeks, but it cannot guarantee the quantity. The largest customer has threatened to cancel all future orders, which would cost the firm half its revenue, while the smaller customers have said they will wait if they are told honestly how long the delay will be.
items.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strongly support allocating the scarce chips fairly across all customers rather than giving them all to the largest customer?

A week later, the chip shipment has arrived: enough chips for 40 percent of planned production. The largest customer ordered 50 percent of planned output, three smaller customers together ordered 30 percent, and the online store was to take 20 percent. If the firm allocates the available chips in proportion to orders, how many percent of planned production will the largest customer receive, and how many percent will the online store receive?
options: 50 percent for the largest customer and 20 percent for the online store
40 percent for the largest customer and 20 percent for the online store
25 percent for the largest customer and 10 percent for the online store
20 percent for the largest customer and 8 percent for the online store
20 percent for the largest customer and 20 percent for the online store
items.explanation: Only 40 percent of planned production can be made, so each customer receives 40 percent of its own order. The largest customer ordered 50 percent, and 40 percent of 50 percent is 20 percent of planned production. The online store ordered 20 percent, and 40 percent of 20 percent is 8 percent. The 50 and 20 option is what the customers ordered, not what they receive, and 25 and 10 wrongly divides the available chips equally among four parties.

items.question: The next shipment has arrived and supply has recovered. The board now asks for a rule that will stop a single chip from ever deciding the firm's production again. Which rule does BOTH things: it stops any product from depending on a single chip supplier, and it keeps a buffer stock equal to one quarter's production of every specialised chip?
options: The firm will give all available chips to its largest customer in every shortage, whatever the smaller customers say
No product may depend on a single chip supplier, and the firm will keep a buffer stock equal to one quarter's production of every specialised chip
The firm will keep no buffer stock, so that cash is never tied up in chips
The firm will promise every customer full delivery, whatever the chip supply
No product may depend on a single chip supplier, but the firm will keep no buffer stock, so that cash is never tied up in chips
items.explanation: The rule must do two things: remove single-supplier dependence, and hold a buffer stock for shortages. Only the second option does both. The last option removes the single-supplier dependence but keeps no buffer stock, so it fails the second condition. Giving all chips to the largest customer abandons the smaller ones, keeping no buffer stock leaves the firm exposed, and promising full delivery whatever the supply is a promise the firm cannot keep.

If the tracking data was sold to advertisers, the harm is concrete and the consent was never given, which makes the case for stopping the tracking decisive. The app being popular and parents liking the reports do not cure the lack of consent. A rival doing the same does not make it acceptable. The privacy policy mentioning partners in dense language is exactly the problem, since parents did not understand it.
options: The app is popular with parents who like the progress reports
The tracking data was sold to advertisers who target children with ads for games and snacks
A rival learning app also tracks how long children spend on each lesson
The privacy policy mentions sharing data with partners in dense legal language
The app is free for all schools that use it
items.passage: A learning app used by 5 lakh school children records how long each child spends on every lesson, which questions the child gets wrong, and the child's location while using the app. The app is free for schools, and its revenue comes from selling insights to advertisers and to publishers who want to know what children find difficult. The app's sign-up screen asks parents to agree to a long privacy policy, but the screen does not explain in plain language that children's learning data is sold. A journalist has found that the data includes enough detail to identify individual children when combined with school records, and has asked the company for a comment before publishing. The product head argues that the data helps publishers make better textbooks, that the app is free only because of this revenue, and that parents agreed to the policy. The child safety officer warns that selling children's data without clear consent breaches the trust of schools and parents, and that a regulator could ban the app from schools. The founders must decide before the journalist publishes, because the story will reach every school that uses the app. The journalist has given the company 48 hours to comment before publishing, and the story will reach every school that uses the app. The app is used in 2,000 schools and its progress reports are sent to parents every week. The child safety officer has warned that a regulator could ban the app from schools if children's data was sold without clear consent. The founders have told staff that the app will stay free only if the data revenue continues, and the company has no other source of income.
items.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strongly support stopping the sale of children's learning data?
items.set_title: DM2: The Learning App and Children's Data
DM2: The Learning App and Children's Data
items.question: A day later, the journalist has given the company 48 hours to comment before publishing, and the story will reach every school that uses the app. Five facts have come to light. (A) The app records how long each child spends on every lesson, which questions the child gets wrong, and the child's location while using the app. (B) The data includes enough detail to identify individual children when combined with school records. (C) The app is free for schools only because of the revenue from selling insights to advertisers and publishers. (D) The child safety officer warns that selling children's data without clear consent breaches the trust of schools and parents, and that a regulator could ban the app from schools. (E) The sign-up screen asks parents to agree to a long privacy policy, but does not explain in plain language that children's learning data is sold. Which combination of three facts MOST helps the founders stop selling the data at once and tell schools plainly what was sold?
options: (A), (C) and (E)
(B), (C) and (D)
(A), (B) and (D)
(C), (D) and (E)
(B), (D) and (E)
items.explanation: Stopping the sale is justified by three legs: the data can identify individual children (B), the regulator could ban the app from schools (D), and parents never gave clear consent because the screen did not explain the sale in plain language (E). (A) describes what is recorded, which is true but does not by itself show the harm, and (C) argues for continuing the sale, since it describes the revenue it brings. Every distractor triple contains two right facts and one that points the wrong way.

items.set_title: DM2: The Learning App and Children's Data
items.question: The founders have stopped the sale and told the schools. The board now asks for a rule that will stop children's data from ever being sold again. Which rule best prevents a recurrence?
options: Children's data will be sold only to publishers, because publishers make better textbooks
The privacy policy will be made longer, so that parents are less likely to read it
Parents will be asked to agree to a long policy, with no plain-language explanation, as before
Children's data will never be sold, and any data sharing with a third party will need plain-language consent from parents, approved by the child safety officer, before it begins
The founders will decide data sales in private, without telling the child safety officer
items.explanation: A ban plus plain-language consent approved by the safety officer attacks both causes: the sale itself and the consent that was never informed. Selling only to publishers repeats the sale, a longer policy repeats the unreadable consent, and deciding in private repeats the governance failure.

If the winning team used a leaked case from a previous year, the win was obtained unfairly and the case for disqualification is direct. The team being from a famous school and the judges praising the presentation do not cure cheating. A sponsor wanting a quick decision is a pressure, not a justification. The dean being new does not change the facts.
options: The winning team comes from a famous business school
The judges praised the winning team's presentation style
The main sponsor wants a decision before the press conference
The dean is new and wants to avoid controversy in the first year
The winning team used a leaked copy of the case from a previous year that other teams did not have
items.passage: A business school runs a national case competition with 40 teams and a prize of 10 lakh rupees, sponsored by a large bank. After the final, the organisers learn that the winning team may have received the case study in advance from a former student who now works at the sponsor bank. The evidence is a set of messages that suggest the team saw the case two days early, but the messages do not prove it beyond doubt. The dean must decide whether to disqualify the winning team, order a fresh final with a new case, or let the result stand. Disqualifying the team would embarrass the sponsor and the school, and the team has already been announced as the winner in the press. Ordering a fresh final would cost 15 lakh rupees and would be unfair to the other finalists who prepared for the original case. Letting the result stand would keep the sponsor happy but would leave the other 39 teams believing the competition was rigged. The dean has 48 hours before the prize ceremony, and the runner-up team has already written to the dean demanding an investigation. The runner-up team has written to the dean demanding an investigation and has shared its letter with the other finalists. The sponsor bank has said it wants the prize ceremony to go ahead as planned and has warned that a public dispute would damage its brand. The competition has run for 12 years and has never faced a cheating allegation before. The dean has 48 hours before the ceremony, and the winning team has already been announced in the press and on the school's website.
items.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strongly support disqualifying the winning team?

A day later, the runner-up team has written demanding an investigation and has shared its letter with the other finalists. The sponsor bank has said it wants the prize ceremony to go ahead as planned. Five facts have come to light. (A) The evidence is a set of messages suggesting the winning team saw the case two days early, but the messages do not prove it beyond doubt. (B) The winning team has already been announced as the winner in the press and on the school's website. (C) Ordering a fresh final would cost 15 lakh rupees and would be unfair to the other finalists who prepared for the original case. (D) Letting the result stand would leave the other 39 teams believing the competition was rigged. (E) The competition has run for 12 years and has never faced a cheating allegation before. Which combination of three facts MOST helps the dean order an independent investigation before the prize ceremony, rather than disqualifying the team or letting the result stand?
options: (A), (B) and (E)
(B), (C) and (D)
(A), (C) and (D)
(A), (B) and (D)
(C), (D) and (E)
items.explanation: An investigation is justified by three legs: the evidence is suggestive but not conclusive, so neither disqualification nor exoneration is justified yet (A); a fresh final would be unfair and costly (C); and letting the result stand would leave 39 teams believing the competition was rigged (D). (B) is about the announcement, which is a reason to act carefully rather than to investigate, and (E) is history that makes the allegation surprising but does not decide what to do. Every distractor triple contains two right facts and one that does not support the investigation.

items.question: The investigation has found that the winning team did receive the case early, and the prize has been awarded to the runner-up. The school now asks for a rule that will stop a leak from ever deciding a competition again. Which rule best prevents a recurrence?
options: Case studies will be released to all teams at the same moment, the source of any leak will be investigated by someone outside the organising team, and no team may receive the case from a sponsor employee
The winning team will be disqualified whenever anyone alleges cheating, whether or not there is evidence
The sponsor bank will be allowed to share the case with any team it chooses
The competition will be cancelled whenever an allegation is made, whatever the evidence
The organisers will keep the case secret from all teams until the final, so that nobody can prepare
items.explanation: Releasing the case to everyone at the same moment, investigating leaks independently and barring sponsor employees from sharing it attacks all three causes. Disqualifying on any allegation punishes the innocent, and keeping the case secret until the final makes preparation impossible.

If the two managers' teams have the highest attrition in the firm, the feud is already costing the firm its people, which strengthens the case for intervening now. Both managers being talented and both having long service explain why the firm hesitates, but do not show the feud is harmless. A client liking one manager is a reason to keep that person, not to ignore the conflict. The feud being about strategy is a description, not evidence that it is harmless.
options: Both managers are talented and have been with the firm for over ten years
The feud is about business strategy, not about personal issues
The two managers' teams have the highest staff attrition in the firm, with 12 people leaving in the last year
A major client likes working with one of the managers
Both managers have strong support among senior leadership
items.passage: Two senior managers in a consulting firm have been in open conflict for a year. One leads the digital practice and the other leads the traditional advisory practice, and each publicly criticises the other's work in front of clients and junior staff. Their teams have stopped sharing information, two joint projects have failed because the managers refused to cooperate, and 12 people have left the firm in the last year, most of them citing the conflict. The managing partner has so far avoided intervening, because both managers bring in large revenues and each has strong support among the partners. The human resources head warns that the conflict is now the main reason for attrition, that clients have noticed the tension, and that junior staff are afraid to work across the two practices. The managing partner must decide before the annual partner meeting, where the two managers are expected to argue again in front of all partners. The options are to mediate between them with a clear agreement, to separate their responsibilities completely, to remove one of them from a leadership role, or to do nothing and hope the conflict resolves itself. The managing partner has avoided intervening for a year because both managers bring in large revenues and each has strong support among the partners. The annual partner meeting is in three weeks, and the two managers are expected to argue again in front of all 40 partners. The human resources head has records of the 12 departures and of the two joint projects that failed when the managers refused to cooperate. Junior staff have told the human resources head they are afraid to work across the two practices.
items.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strongly support intervening now rather than waiting?
items.set_title: DM4: The Two Managers at War
DM4: The Two Managers at War
items.question: A year later, the managing partner has kept records: 12 people left in the last year, most citing the conflict, and two joint projects failed because the managers refused to cooperate. Each departure costs the firm about 20 lakh rupees in recruitment and lost work, and each failed joint project cost about 50 lakh rupees. If the firm had mediated at a cost of 30 lakh rupees and the mediation would have prevented half the departures and both failed projects, how much would the firm have saved, net of the mediation cost?
options: 1.9 crore rupees
2.2 crore rupees
2.5 crore rupees
1.6 crore rupees
3.1 crore rupees
items.explanation: The conflict cost 12 departures at 20 lakh rupees, which is 2.4 crore rupees, plus two failed projects at 50 lakh rupees, which is 1 crore rupee, a total of 3.4 crore rupees. Mediation would have prevented half the departures, saving 6 times 20 lakh, which is 1.2 crore rupees, and both failed projects, saving 1 crore rupee, a gross saving of 2.2 crore rupees. Less the 30 lakh rupee cost of mediation, the net saving is 1.9 crore rupees. The 2.2 option forgets the mediation cost, and the 3.1 option wrongly counts the full conflict cost as saved.

The managing partner has avoided intervening for a year because both managers bring in large revenues and each has strong support among the partners. items.question: The managing partner decides to mediate between the two managers. Which of the following, if true, would most strongly support mediation over removing one manager from a leadership role?
options: Both managers bring in large revenues and each has strong support among the partners, so removing either would split the partnership and lose clients.
12 people have left the firm in the last year, most of them citing the conflict.
Clients have noticed the tension between the two managers.
Junior staff are afraid to work across the two practices.
The two managers are expected to argue again at the annual partner meeting.
items.explanation: The departures, the client tension, the frightened juniors and the coming meeting all show that action is needed, but they support any strong action, including removal.
